utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. And welcome back for what we expect will be an uninterrupted run until the summer recess. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. For the Office of the Prosecutor, I'm Tom Hannis, with Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a matter, Your Honour, that I wish to raise this morning. You will -- you're probably aware I sent an e-mail yesterday morning, notifying the -- our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber of the situation. As I explained everything in the -- in that particular mail, I will just shortly review the contents of it. You will remember, Your Honours, that on two occasions in April, on April 11 and April 14, I first agreed to provide the Trial Chamber and the parties with all the statements made by our witnesses. At that point, and on one other occasion, I informed the Trial Chamber that except for the statement of Nikola Milanovic there are no other statements or investigator's notes or records of interview or tape-recorded interviews of our witnesses. It is with a sincere regret that I must now inform you that the representations that I made in court were incorrect. Namely, we have found one statement and three records of the witness interview. The documents have been disclosed yesterday, one -- the moment when we found these -- these documents, we sent them for translations, and one of the -- one of the records of interview has been translated already and has been filed -- has been filed with the Office of the Prosecutor and a copy to the Trial Chamber. The other three, one statement and two records of the interview, are in the process of translation and we are sure that it will be translated in the course of this week. Your Honours, I -- I trust you will understand that I accept full responsibility, and, again, I offer my sincere apologies to the Trial Chamber and Office of the Prosecutor. This confusion and miscommunication on my part was not at all intended to mislead either the Trial Chamber or the Office of the Prosecutor. That is -- that is what I had to inform the Trial Chamber about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please forgive me for being unaware of the mail that you have sent to us at this point. I hadn't seen those statements or interviews so my question to you at this point is: To whom were these statements given and -- or who took the interviews with those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- I sent the mail yesterday morning with my letter to the Office of the Prosecutor. I copied the letter to the Trial Chamber, together with the -- with all the records of the interviews and the statement which we found in our records. The records of the interview were done by Mr. -- my co-counsel Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic, and the statement was given by Mr. Drano Vlaco. And the other three are Witness Orasanin, Bjelosevic, and Macar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And to whom were these statements given?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the records of the interviews conducted between the counsel for the Defence and the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I understood. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the next step in this would the completion of the translations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. We sent it for translation and I'm pretty sure that it will be this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks. Are there any other preliminary matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there's one from our side. This -- I'd like to make a submission in addition to the oral submissions that were made on the 13th and 14th of April; that's the first and second day of the Bjelosevic testimony. On the 13th, Mr. Zecevic made an oral application, and there's no written submission, an oral application concerning Rule 66(B), where we said that there had been a violation of Rule 66(B) in relation to Bjelosevic. That was on the first day of his testimony. The next day, at the beginning of the session, the 14th, Ms. Korner replied orally, and at that time she acknowledged there had been violations of Rule 66(B). The only point I wish to make is that we did not specifically address what we considered to be the appropriate remedy for that violation. And that's what I'll do right now. We say that because of the non-compliance with Rule 66(B), the -- Mr. Stanisic did not receive the requested material prior to the testimony of Bjelosevic. We say that Rule 66(B) is tied to Article 21(4)(b), which is the right enshrined in the Statute to have adequate time and facilities to prepare the Defence. We say that the appropriate remedy would be to preclude the Prosecution from using these documents during its cross-examination of Bjelosevic. We're not entitled -- we were precluded from having them prior to his testimony and we say that as a result of the non-compliance with 66(B), the Prosecution should not be allowed to use them during their cross-examination of Bjelosevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Zecevic informed us in advance this was going to be the application this morning. Your Honours, we resist it. Your Honours may recall that although we did agree that we had been specifically asked for documents authored by Mr. Bjelosevic, we'd actually missed some. But as Your Honours will recall, when we -- when I went through the documents on the Thursday, the 14th of April, most, if not all, appeared on the Defence's list of documents because they themselves had been provided with the documents by Mr. Bjelosevic. So, at the moment, Your Honours, we say that there's no prejudice to the Defence for this lapse, which we admit, on our parts, in failing to discover the documents. We also say that it is an excessive sanction that we should be precluded from using any of these documents in cross-examination. But, in any event, it may well be that Your Honours will find this difficult, as I will, to rule upon this - not that I will be ruling, Your Honours' ruling, but my only -- application we make - without being provided of a list of documents that the Defence say we should not be allowed to use in cross-examination. And it may be that we'll have to revisit this matter perhaps before Mr. Bjelosevic returns on the 16th of May. So, Your Honours, that's all that I want to say on that matter at the moment. Your Honours, while I'm on my feet, can I, however, mention something else. I don't know whether Your Honours have seen the motion that the Defence filed saying that we should be compelled to comply with Rule 66(B). They filed a motion on the 28th of April which, I think, was Thursday. Yes. Thursday of last week. Having earlier sent us a request which they put with the motion in an annex, including our response and a much, much earlier request dating back to October of 2009. We responded on the same day, that is, last Thursday, the 28th, saying we had made our position clear in our response but also adding in our response the original reply to the first motion -- not the first motion, the -- one of the first letters they filed. There has been other requests made since then but that was the major one. However, Your Honours, it seems to me, I'm afraid, that this is one that Your Honours will have to deal with fairly quickly, because effectively what we say is that this is not a proper request under 66(B); this is merely an attempt to preclude the Prosecution from, as it were, keeping its powder dry, if you like, until, as the Court has ordered, we should reveal what documents we're going to use for cross-examination after the witness has gone into the witness box. But that's all I want to say about that matter. But can we ask that Your Honours rule fairly quickly because obviously this is going to affect upcoming witnesses quite dramatically. And finally, Your Honours, again the Defence have filed an application either for reconsideration or for leave to appeal Your Honours's ruling in respect of Dr. Nielsen. As Your Honours know, that was all filed confidentially. But I'm raising it now. It may be that again that's something else that ought to be dealt with with some expedition and it may affect the present witness and/or cross-examination of that witness. So those are the matters that we want to raise this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. If I may return to the first matter: Do I understand your position to be that you are requesting that the motion made by Mr. O'Sullivan this morning be fleshed out in order for you to be in a position to - I don't want to use the word "intelligently," but that's the only word that comes to mind - respond to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, it's not -- I don't know what -- it's not really a motion. It's effectively -- it's adding to what was said before, namely that they, the Defence, assert that Your Honours should punish the Prosecution by preventing use of these documents in -- in cross-examination. We say at the moment we'd like a list of the documents they say we are precluded from using in cross-examination. That would enable us to see which of them that we know to be in the Defence possession. And in all likelihood because we know that Mr. Bjelosevic gave more to the Defence than has actually been put into their list of documents, because that's effectively what was said. So it may well be that they've got all the documents and had all the documents in any event in advance. So I, -- in effect, I'm asking the Defence not only to indicate which documents, and which documents they say they never had, and how they are prejudiced by those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So there are obviously a number of matters which are going to engage our attention out of court in order -- especially the two matters you've indicated are -- have some urgency to them. Yes, thanks. So could we have the next witness escorted in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our next witness is Professor Bajagic, our police expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While we're waiting, can I just make an inquiry through Your Honours. Mr. Bjelosevic was supposed to have been handing over documents to VWS. Do we have any update on whether that's happened? Because, if not, it should happen fairly quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The Court Officer informs us that those documents have not yet been returned to -- handed over to VWS, but there is a process which the -- which has been --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: They're being handed over to the witness today. There is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- that we had refined after the last adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we expect them fairly soon once they're handed over, because obviously we've got to go through them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajagic. First of all, do you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to give, to read, the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that you are about to make does expose you to the penalty of perjury, should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now, then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated. Could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Mladen Bajagic. I was born on the 5th of April, 1962, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I work as professor at the Academy of Criminal Science and Policing in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, since I was born in Sarajevo, from the beginning of the war I was member of the National Security Service in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this your first testimony before this Tribunal or have you given testimony before another Tribunal in your country about the -- the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my second appearance before this Tribunal. I testified in the Popovic et al. case as an expert witness. That was some two, two and a half years ago. Outside this Tribunal, I never testified about anything that happened during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So then I only have to remind you of the proceedings before this Tribunal since you know about them. You have been called as a expert witness by the Defence of Mr. Stanisic. Mr. Zecevic who is sitting on your left, sitting on your left-hand side, and he has asked for 15 hours to do his examination-in-chief. After that, Mr. Krgovic, the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, sitting on your left as well, will cross-examine you for -- How many time, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our estimate is two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For two hours, more or less. And after that there is the cross-examination of the Office of the Prosecutor, sitting on your right-hand side, and they ask for 15 hours as well. After that, and in the mean time, Judges can -- no, after the cross-examination we give the floor back to Mr. Zecevic for final questions eventually, and after that, and in between, the Judges can ask questions as well. As a practical matter, for recordings, et cetera, we sit in sessions of 90 minutes with each time 20 minutes' break, and morning sessions end at a quater to 2.00. That's all for the moment. So I'll give the floor to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one more thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, when we filed our notice concerning this witness testifying as an expert, we indicated that we had certain objections as to his expertise in the scope of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I'm coming to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now a Ruling on that matter: The Trial Chamber finds that Mladen Bajagic is properly characterised as an expert within the meaning of Rule 94 bis and the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. The Tribunal, however, takes note of the Prosecution's 94 bis B notice filed on the 19th of April, 2011, whereby the Prosecution submitted that it does not accept Mladen Bajagic's expertise report. In accordance with the practice in -- in the instant case, the Trial Chamber will make a decision on the admission into evidence of Mladen Bajagic report at the end of this testimony. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic. Can you hear me? I said good morning.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you stated some basic information when you were asked by the Trial Chamber. I would now like to ask you to give some more detailed information about your training and the scholarly work you are engaged in currently.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As I said, I was born in Sarajevo on the 5th of April, 1962. In Sarajevo, I graduated from primary and secondary school, "Gymnasija," and the Faculty of Political Science from which I graduated in 1988. After that, I did some work in journalism and I worked also on the socio-political communities that were then in existence in the old political system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but not fully professionally. And as for my scholarly career: From 1996 to 2000, I followed a master's course at the Faculty of Political Science in Belgrade. And later on I got my Ph.D. from the same faculty in Belgrade, in international relations, and thereby I'm now entitled to the title of Ph.D. From the beginning of my academic career, I have worked at the police academy and the post-secondary school of the interior in Belgrade. As a result of the process of integration, the Academy of Criminal Science and Policing was founded, and I work there at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I apologise. I think that it isn't clearly recorded what you are talking about. Could you please repeat which two institutions you worked for that were later merged. Please explain slowly.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The first institution where I worked as an assistant professor was the Police Academy of Belgrade. At the post-secondary school of the interior, I also worked as lecturer, senior lecturer, and professor. These two institutions were integrated a few years ago in -- as part of the Bologna Process and were merged into the Academy of Criminal Science and Policing. I worked there -- I worked there as a lecturer, and currently I'm a extraordinary professor, teaching several courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, I see that Mr. Hannis wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to bring to Mr. Zecevic's attention the transcript at line -- at page 12, line 3. I think it's an error, and he may want to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, where did you get your Ph.D., from which faculty or institution, and when exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I got my Ph.D. at the Faculty of Political Science, the International Relations Department, and I specialised in security sciences in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please explain --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Could you now please continue to explain which courses you teach now.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The institutions that I mentioned, two of them, and the political police academy, are organisations where I covered many areas and taught a number of courses. What I'm covering currently are the following areas. They are -- or, rather, at the basic level academic studies, fourth year, I teach two courses: The first one is the methodology of intelligence work; and the other, international security. At the master's studies level, within the same institution, I teach terrorism and political violence. And finally, at the academic specialist studies level, I teach three courses: These three are intelligence and counter-intelligence aspects of terrorism and anti-terrorism; the second is comparative models of the protection of persons and property; and finally, the third, security systems. Before these courses, within the first two institutions I mentioned, I taught the following courses: basics of security; the system of state or national security. And that is what's important for the institutions where I worked permanently and where I still work. As is the custom in the academic community, I have repeatedly held lectures as a guest professor and an engaged professor, based on a work contract, and in that capacity I have also taught at other institutions of higher education. One of the most important courses I have taught there is security management and another being security systems. I think that would be it, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. Could you briefly mention whether you have written any monographies or other works and which ones are the most significant you have written?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As for my career so far, my career as a professor, that is, I have published two textbooks and five monographs and between 90 and 100 papers, both home and abroad. These papers were published in scholarly journals or in different publications that were the result of different international conferences. Perhaps I could single out a few of these books. As for textbooks, I published two of them: One is entitled, "The Fundamentals of Security" and "The Methodology of Intelligence." As for monographs, I have published the following: "The Role of the Intelligence Community in the Foreign Policy of the United States of America." I think that the date was 2004, but it doesn't really matter, the date, I mean. Then, "The Security of the World from a Secret to a Public Nature." So that is the second title. And the last one is: "Espionage in the 21st Century: Contemporary Intelligence and Security Systems." That is what I can say as far as textbooks and monographs are concerned. As for individual papers, there were a great deal of them. If I really need to focus on that, I would have to give it an extra thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. Thank you. This will do. Mr. Bajagic, tell me, did you attend any special courses and, if so, which courses were they and who organised them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Already in the year 2000 and afterwards, the institutions where I worked developed a truly fruitful cooperation with many international institutions, especially the OSCE. The OSCE organised the most important courses that I attended, along with other colleagues, lecturers from institutions of higher learning. I attended a three-month course that was entitled "Training the Trainers," and it had to do with police work. And then there was yet another course that took place in Basdorf in Germany, and that was a sequel to that first course. And as a result of that, we received certificates, certifying that we could train trainers; namely, that we were thereby specialised to train those who trained police forces. Of course, there were also courses organised by the International Red Cross, but I have singled out the most important courses I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the Red Cross. Did you attend any course related to international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for not having stated that specifically. It was precisely that course that was organised by the International Red Cross in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you do have your report there, don't you, the report that you have prepared for this case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bajagic, this report that is in front of you, that is entitled, "The Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, Beginnings, Purview, Jurisdiction, Organisation, and Control, 1990 to 1993," who prepared this report? Who's the author of this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Of course, I am the author of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bajagic, did you prepare this report all by yourself in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I authored the entire report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, who assigned this task to you? Who gave you the topic for this report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As for this task -- or, rather, the first tentative topic for this report was given to me by the Defence team of Mr. Stanisic, That is to say, yourself and your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, in addition to the request and the topic itself that was provided to you by the Defence, what else did you receive from the Defence of Mr. Stanisic? What other documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The Defence team provided me with the general topic that I was supposed to investigate. And I can say that the title, as you see it here, is a result of my research. Of course, first there is a working title, but it was finally formulated this way towards the very end. As for my topic of research, I received relevant documents on the basis of which I was to write this report. I understand this as raw material for my research work, and that is what I received from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the report has 494 or 495 footnotes that pertain to the documents that were used when compiling this piece of research. Who selected these documents?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I received from the Defence team a certain number of documents. And then as I prepared and planned this research project, I categorised the documents. However, in addition to the documents provided to me by the Defence, as I dealt with particular topics that are important for certain parts of this paper, I also made an effort to find certain documents that helped me in writing this report, this expert report, in the best possible way. So, of course, there are many studies and monographs that I referred to and that are listed in the footnotes, many more than provided to me by the Defence originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who selected the documents that would be used for your expert report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I received a group of documents, but then I selected the documents for the report myself. For me, this expert report is just like a research project, as far as I'm concerned. So it requires a clear, methodological procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but before we get to methodology and procedures, let us dwell on this particular question now. Mr. Bajagic, did you receive from the Defence the expert report of Professor Nielsen who was a Prosecution expert in this case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. As I've already pointed out, I was an expert in this Court before, in a different case, so I already had occasion to read Mr. Nielsen's report, but, yes, I did have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, were you here for a while when Professor Nielsen testified as a Prosecution expert?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was here and I followed his testimony for a few days. I think it was in December 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic -- or, rather, just a moment, please. Could you please open your report, look at the second page, that's where we see the contents. Just a moment, please, I'll give you -- or, rather, I'll provide a reference for e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D06-2404, page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, could you please explain to us what it is that we see before us now. And could you explain the document that we see on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: These are the detailed contents of this expert report. As you can see, there are a few broad subjects. And finally, there are 12 attachments, annexes. I don't know whether I should explain each and every general subject involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you can explain what they pertain to.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The first general subject within this expert report is entitled, "Constituting of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Establishment of Organs of State Authority." Then there are a few subheadings such as, "General Characteristics of the Political and State Crisis in BH --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a question, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why you included this particular item in your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Doing research into the establishment or the determination of the remit, organisation, and control of such a complex system as the Ministry of the Interior in the executive branch of government of any country is impossible unless you outline the realistic context, which I did. The Ministry of the Interior is part of the state authorities in the executive branch of government, and with regard to the specific circumstances in which this Ministry of the Interior developed, the one about which I wrote this expert report, namely, the Serbian Republic of BH and its Ministry of the Interior, and also with regard to the political crisis that prevailed then, it was impossible to do research about its organisation, mission, and so on, unless you position it in the broader context, the way I did. That's simply part of my methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain chapter 2.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You mean the chapter Roman II?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It's entitled, "The MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina between 1990 and April 1992." The Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina grew out of the system of this MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH, and the period stated here, from 1990 till 1992, has more clearly defined my efforts to describe the way of functioning of the authorities of the Socialist Republic of BH until the well-known events in April 1992. I also went into the reasons for the gradual decentralisation and the coming into being of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is my explanation of the second chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please explain the following chapter.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The following chapter is entitled, "The Functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of BH in the Period from April to December 1992." Clearly, this is the basic chapter, the most important one, that comprises broad issues such as the legal framework and the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior in the system of the executive branch of government; namely, the de jure aspect. Of course, we also had to deal with the -- the surreal situation and the organisation of the ministry in 1992. Some issues were more pronounced with regard to the tasks of the ministry, and that's why I tried to describe these issues in a systematic manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain the following chapter as stated in the contents, and please explain why it is a separate chapter.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The internal organisation of any ministry of interior, including this one, is the basis upon which it acts within the legal framework that defines its scope. In the legal system in the former SFRY and the countries that emerged subsequently, these matters were always dealt with through the rule-book on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. This is a separate chapter here because in the relevant period, namely in the first year of its existence as the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its basic structure was defined by rule-books that were created earlier, that is, in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But then there was an initiative to draft a new rule-book for the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of BH. That is very important because that rule-book lays down in detail the organisation and the territorial structure of the entire Ministry of the Interior. And the remit of the individual organisational units are defined. There are many significant matters that are dealt with there, and that's why this is a separate chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, in your opinion, is it possible to write such a report about the Ministry of the Interior -- or, rather, which rules and regulations are the most important ones for the understanding and clear classification, if I may say, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: When I was explaining the chapter about the internal organisation of the MUP, especially the legal framework, I omitted to say, but I can say it now, that an objective and systematic manner of dealing with matters pertaining to the work of the Ministry of the Interior, it is necessary, always considering the Constitution as the highest legal document of a country, also presenting a number of other pieces of legislation [as interpreted]. And that has been done in this expert report. I'm specifically referring to the Law on the Government, then the Law on Public Administration, the Law on Ministries, and the Law on the Interior. That is the legal framework that was adopted in early 1992, in the Serb Republic of BH. Clearly it is outright impossible to analyse all the provisions of these laws unless we also consider the legislation of the former SFRY, including the Socialist Republic of BH. These are the same laws and regulations that I mentioned when I spoke about the Serb Republic of BH. But because of the specific political and general situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, it was necessary to go into some provisions of the Law on Defence, the Law on the Armed Forces and, of course, something that constitutes the historic background, the Law on All People's Defence and the Strategy of All People's Defence that were in force for -- in all of the former SFRY. These are the central pieces of legislation that I also consulted because I deem it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain the correlation of -- or, rather, between what you call the Law on the Interior and the rule-book on the internal organisation of the MUP? What is the correlation between these two pieces of legislation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The Law on the Interior clearly defines the mission and the vision of the MUP and its scope of work. Naturally, it defines the remit of the ministry, but the law only deals with the organisation of the MUP at a general level. And it's the rule-book, a piece of subordinate legislation, that goes into the details of the structures of the ministry and the remit of the individual organisational units, as well as the rights and duties of these units in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please comment on chapter IV of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This chapter is entitled, "Disciplinary and Criminal Responsibility of RS MUP Staff in 1992." It was part of my assignment. All rules and regulations and subordinate legislation also deal with these matters that are very important for the functioning of the ministry. This disciplinary and criminal responsibility was here analysed by consulting the Law on the Interior of the Serb Republic, as compared to the rules and regulations that were in force in the socialist republic, and this is the way how I tried to give a brief overview of how members of the ministry could be held -- could be held responsible for their acts or omissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And please give us a short explanation of the annexes. What are they about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Working on the individual chapters and the expert report as a whole, I came across some documents I considered extremely important for the understanding of both the Ministry of the Interior and the general context in which it came into being. So as not to overburden the report with footnotes, I considered it much more effective to enclose some documents in the report itself, and I only refer to them in the footnotes. I believe that this -- it is much easier to understand why these documents were enclosed. There's a total of 12 annexes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain to us Annex 12. What does it refer to and why did you include it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Annex 12 was created as a result of the Defence's wish from the -- from earlier this year about the task of the -- tasks of the army and the police during the state of the imminent threat of war. And I invested a significant effort to explain some topics that deal with subordination. And then I also had to go into the issues of coordination and acting in coordination, from the point of view of national security, and this is the last annex which I included upon the request of the Defence. All the others I included of my own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, sir, can you explain which methodology you used in drafting this report? Please explain very briefly. And if you use any technical terms, do explain what they mean.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The methodology of researching social matters or the research methodology in the humanities is unique in the entire world. There's a single methodology. Since the Ministry of the Interior, by definition, is one of the protagonists of national security, with regard to what I said about original documents, the -- setting up such a complex system of public administration required a multi-disciplinary approach. If you do research into such an institution or such a process, political -- which is a political, legal -- and legal phenomenon, and because of that I had to adhere to very strict methodological rules from the very beginning. The first task was the classification of sources, the sources that I had before me. By their subject matter, their nature, their contents, and it was necessary to devise a codex of classification into various sets. As for the methods themselves, you can tell at first sight that this is about a qualitative and quantitative analysis of contents; then analysis and synthesis; induction and deduction; the comparative method, and, of course, this includes the sociological and legal method; and many other techniques that are required to deal with a document systematically. In principle, this expert report is the result of -- is -- of a scholarly process, which it, indeed, was. I defined hypotheses; I defined indicators as material indicators of what could be found in the de facto and de jure sets of the individual problems dealt with; and, of course, the well-known logical processes such as proving, disproving, et cetera. Since this is a multi-disciplinary problem, a very wide range of general, basic methods and other methodological techniques were applied in the process of drafting this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "multi-disciplinary problem," can you briefly explain what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. A multi-disciplinary approach to studying the work of the ministry was indispensable because the ministry is part of the executive government, and we are dealing with the legal framework, so that we would see what the de jure situation was. The Ministry of the Interior, as an institution or as a problem that we are studying, has all the characterises of a political, legal, sociological, and any other phenomenon because it is quite simply impossible to view it from a single angle only. It is indispensable to carry out a political analysis as well because you cannot look at it separately. You have to look at it within a political and security-related context within which it developed. That is why I said that this did, indeed, require a multi-disciplinary approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, and I think it's a proper time that we take the adjournment now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honours forgive me if I leave court now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, one more question relating to the methodology. Can you explain to us the mechanism on the basis of which scientific conclusions are drawn, and which particular mechanism did you apply in your work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Scientific conclusions, or one's views, are created generally on the basis of the problem that you face and the subject that you research. In this particular instance, this was the Ministry of the Interior. In view of the available sources, you do that, and you also use them as indicators, and you apply them to the entire hypothetical framework, from the general to the specific theses, and also the very terms of reference creates also a basis for certain conclusions. Therefore, you have to make cross-reference between various sources about one specific problem that can then lead you to reaching a specific conclusion. And at that you try to reach as high a degree of reliability as possible. And you sometimes have some impressions about the problem, because it is not always possible to arrive at definitive conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is the drawing of conclusions dependant on, let's say, the volume or the quantity of positive indicators that you receive with respect to a specific problem? Let me be a little bit clearer: Do you arrive at conclusions by taking a whole set of documents relating to a specific topic you determine a certain common denominator, which serves as a basis for your conclusion, or did you apply some different method?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That is precisely so. Through these process of thinking, proving, and disproving, you eventually arrive at a set of documents that create a common denominator that indicate a specific conclusion. It is impossible to arrive at opinions and views based on a sole decision. Any kind of research in this area you need to have a number of documents in order to arrive at a relevant conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, what is the situation if you have a number of documents confirming one common denominator and then have you another set of documents that disprove it? How do you act in that particular situation with respect to drawing your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Mr. Bajagic, before you go on to answer Mr. Zecevic's question, I think it would be helpful if you could clarify, then, what was, in your view, the common denominator that you found in the studies that you made. You made reference to the possibility of identifying one common denominator in the material that you have analysed. Then Mr. Zecevic then puts it to you the approach that you would take in case you would then find other information that would contradict this common denominator. So my question you to, before you go on to answering

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC'S QUESTION
utterances.text: What was, then, the common denominator that you would base your conclusions on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I arrived at this common denominator, or a general conclusion, at the very end of my research work. It was impossible for me to determine it at the beginning. I could only work with a general hypothesis and that is that the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH truly operated in a very difficult period and which constitutes a time-frame and a framework of this expert report. It is simply impossible to give you a common denominator in one sentence only. That is probably a global conclusion that anyone can arrive at, anyone who reads this report. Speaking about two sides, I said that there was a higher or a lesser degree of probability that can help us to make decisions, but if we strike a balance and if you create something through the codex, it is not up to me to give the ultimate judgement. But each individual problem in my expert report cannot be extracted and viewed out of context. There are some indirect facts and indirect problems that are relating to this report, dealt elsewhere, can also guide us towards certain conclusions. Of course, at any rate, if those confirming a hypothesis overweigh the other argument, and, of course, in other cases we can leave some space for people reading the report to reach at an overall conclusion after reading the report. In that sense, I tried to answer the question to you, Your Honours, and to Mr. Zecevic. I hope I was clear enough. If not, I will try to do it better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We do have your report, and we have read it. I was just trying to give you an opportunity to clarify the conclusions that you have made, which are subject to interpretation. But let's see about that. Let's proceed. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, when I asked you about common denominators, I was referring to specific issues that were dealt with. Can you answer this question: Does every specific issue that you addressed in your expert report and on which you provided conclusions was the subject of each process that you just described in each individual case?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I applied the same methodology in every segment of my report, in each chapter, and it -- in the final part of my report. I always took into account all the facts available in the material that I used when drafting this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to the content of your report itself. In chapter I, entitled, "Constituting of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Establishment of Organs of State Authority," was divided by you into four subsections. Can you summarise what were, in your view, the most important characteristics of the political and state crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina that impacted or that had effect on the subject of your research, i.e., the Ministry of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: If we take a look at the title of chapter I and the four subsections contained therein, one can immediately see that my intention was that I wanted to speak in great detail about the Serbian Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that for that purpose I had to put it into a realistic, social context that prevailed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. As we all know, the general crisis that reigned in the area of the former SFRY was particularly severe in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Multi-party elections that were held in Bosnia-Herzegovina had established all three branches of authority in a way which, at least initially, seemed to provide for a possibility to overcome the problems that were faced in other republics. In view of the fact that there were three political parties taking part in the elections and were victorious, and I'm talking about Party of Democratic Action, the Serbian Democratic Party, and the Croatian Democratic Union, and as a result the authority was established in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it impacted the overall situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including all the state organs and their functioning in B and H. Naturally, the then-Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina found itself in the same context, and we started with problems that were mapped out in this chapter as minor ones, and eventually we reached the main topic, which was the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there are problems listed in this chapter, can you tell us briefly, and maybe you can point us to relevant paragraphs in your work, can you tell us which particular problems you had in mind and why do you think that these specific problems were important?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the basic characteristics of the political crisis in BH, which is from paragraph 1 through paragraph 14, I believed that the best way would be to analyse the activities of these main political entities in that period and their activities, taking into account all the information that I had in front of me but also by resorting to a broader set of material. The intention was particularly to identify the factors that greatly affected the operation of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Through the analysis and research of these problems, many other issues were raised, and it would not have been possible without this first chapter. In spite of the fact that these three parties reached a sort of coalition and inter-party agreement, the available sources indicate, obviously, that on many vital issues the relationships between these entities were at a low level of any sincere cooperation that one might have expected, in view of the coalition that they formed, and that, instead, each one of them made their own moves and their own actions in the context. Now, without going into specifics, I dedicated a number of paragraphs to each of three sides, and I highlighted some of the facts that were of importance in comprehending the operation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you just to try and speak more slowly for the benefit of our interpreters. Thank you. Now, can you just clarify one sentence that you uttered. You said, on page 31, line 5 and 6, that their cooperation was at a much lower level than one would have expected, in view of their coalition agreement, and that, even contrary to that, each of them made certain moves or embarked on certain actions. And as it is translated here, it says "in the context," but I think you said something different; therefore, my question is: Why were these actions or these moves made by each of these three parties and what was the area that it affected the most? Was it the functioning of the state or something else?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: These moves had serious reflections upon the functioning of the state authorities, the government organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "reflections," are you using that term in a positive or negative sense? What is the connotation? I mean, if this is reflected on the functioning of the state organs, is it reflected in terms of these government organs functioning well or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This had an adverse affect on the functioning of the state organs, thereby the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in that period of time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your view, these coalition parties, did every one of them actually want to be the leading party or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: We have a fact here that -- namely, that all three parties won a certain percentage of the vote, and that is how government was established. However, on the basis of certain documents that I analysed, I got the impression that the Party for Democratic Action, in particular, made an effort to exercise dominant influence, especially in those ministries that are called the Ministries of Force in the jargon, the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Justice, and so on, especially the Ministry of Interior. I dealt with that in several paragraphs in particular, and I tried to support it with truly relevant documents as sources that give rise to such statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Following the methodology of your work, we come to the activities of one of these protagonists, if I can put it that way, one of the political parties that you spoke about, that is, the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action. And that is from paragraph 14 to 52, if I'm not mistaken. Can you tell us specifically which actions were taken by that protagonist, resulting, in your view, in a certain significance for the relevance of your own research?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Among others, I observed a few key phenomena as I analysed the activities of the SDA in relation to the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior. Firstly, when analysing certain sources, I came to the conclusion that the Party of Democratic Action showed specific tendencies and took specific action to exercise dominant influence over personnel matters in the Ministry of the Interior in that period, even by violating the intra-party agreement on the distribution of positions within the ministry, starting with the minister and going down to the heads of department. The second conclusion was that they completely neglected the fact that the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had a system of schooling and training in place for decades within its own system. And that, as they interfered in personnel policies directly, they sent many of their party activists to basic training courses in the Republic of Croatia throughout 1991. Later on, they would show up as active members of the MUP and reservists within the MUP already towards the end of 1991. Another problem was the fact that the Party of Democratic Action, although there were already organs established in the field of security in every aspect, already in 1991 they worked on secretly arming a large number of their activists and supporters. That became evident later. This is tellingly demonstrated by the facts that I refer to in my expert report related to the secret establishment of the Patriotic League and other paramilitary formations. And the finale was in the first months of 1992, when the Patriotic League was proclaimed as such, as were other institutions, though, of a military and political narrate, like the military wing of the SDA, the Council for Defence, and so on. Those are some of the basic indicators on the basis of which I drew conclusions that the SDA made efforts even outside the institutions of the system that existed at the time to do something that would significantly assist their political interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, under item 3, you looked at the activity of the other protagonist, if I can put it that way. That is to say, the Croatian party, the HDZ. That is between paragraphs 52 and 80 of your report. If you can summarise this for us very briefly, your conclusion on the action taken by this other coalition partner, the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The HDZ also demonstrated certain aspirations. From the point of view of their own interests, they tried to protect the interests of the Croatian community within Herceg-Bosna -- Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather. However, the HDZ, as one of the victorious parties, not only in 1991 but also in 1990, there are some sources that indicate this, it is already then that they started establishing a particular form of organisation that was then called the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And that is this problem of this third entity, as it were. Although the official date of the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is the 18th of November, 1991, all of 1991 and half of 1990 shows that the top people of Herceg-Bosna were corresponding and indicated that it already existed. So this -- this was also compounded by the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council in the areas where they were predominant. And, of course, the HDZ was closely linked to the HDZ of the Republic of Croatia. They had close cooperation with them with regard to all matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you just clarify one particular thing. The Croatian Defence Council, could you explain what this is all about? What is the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council is a military organisation, right, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which operated as a separate armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now please explain item 4 to us, the activities of the third coalition partner, the SDS. And can you explain, as you did in the previous two cases, what the most important characteristics involved were that affected your research?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Like the other two sides, the SDS, as the political representative of the Serb community in Bosnia-Herzegovina, took certain steps in terms of the political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. Some of the basic characteristics were as follows: The establishment of the autonomous Krajinas and the autonomous regions, already in 1991, in the Autumn of 1991, as far as I can remember. Of course, already in the beginning of 1992, the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted a declaration, passed the constitution of the Serbia Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, an entire set of laws that will be very important in assessing further developments. While analysing all of these three essential political entities, we can say that all of the parties involved made certain moves on the basis of their own interests. And this situation significantly affected the work of the state organs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, ultimately, all the problems that cropped up later. All of this was done more or less in an environment in which, officially, all three political parties were participating in a long-term process of resolving the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina under international auspices. Towards the end of the winter and the beginning of the spring of 1992, this resulted in the adoption of certain documents during the process of the Lisbon Agreement. It was the Cutileiro Agreement, as it has been referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, are you done with this item on the three -- the activities of the three protagonists, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was -- I was going further on this, but, please, Your Honours, by all means, pose a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Professor Bajagic, in this part of your work, the three -- the description of the activities of the three protagonists, as Mr. Zecevic calls it, what strikes me, without even looking to the contents of it, is that for the SDS [sic] your analysis takes 38 pages; for the HDZ, it takes 28 pages; and for the SDS, it takes three pages. Which seems to be rather unbalanced. Is there a logical explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, in the transcript, the SDS is mentioned twice. The first time it's mentioned, it should be "SDA" and not "SDS."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, the report shows that the activities of the political leaders of the SDA has particularly been focussed on, and then the HDZ, and then the SDS. I was guided by a particular methodology, namely, that the latter part of my report would be dedicated to the activities of the Serbian ministry and thereby the Serb side, so de facto and de jure that would have been the case. Perhaps I did not want to burden my report with well-known facts that had already been dealt with in the expert report of Mr. Nielsen. And I did not want to literally copy certain thing. Despite this lack of balance, if we're speaking of the actual number of pages involved, it is important, at least in my view, that I pointed out that all three parties acted on their own, and that is a position that is one that I'm voicing by way of criticism in my report. And this is in line with what Professor Nielsen said. So it's not that something different would happen in the report; it is only due to these facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, you mentioned -- while you were speaking about the contribution to the creation of the crisis by one of the protagonists, the SDS, you mentioned the establishment of these autonomous regions, and before that, you mentioned the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So tell us, please, to what extent that type of regional structure affected the functioning of the state and the state organs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period from 1990 till 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The very fact that these activities are under way until 1992 certainly significantly affect the functioning of the state organs. Probably all state organs functioned difficultly. For an administrative body such as the Ministry of the Interior, this is a special difficulty because that ministry has a specific organisation and hierarchy. And that applies to any country. It's an institution which has a specific remit and area of work. Under such conditions, it is really difficult, when there are inter-party conflicts and a significant inference of politics in their work, to really implement the law and other regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us please take a look at a document. You have these two binders in front of you, and we're interested in the document under tab 27. That's your footnote 71.1. And the document is 1D141. This is a document that is three pages long. Since your footnote is 71.1, please give us a brief explanation what kind of document this is, what it's about, and why you thought it was important to cite it in a footnote in your work.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You stated rightly that this is a document that's three pages long. On page 1, there's a letter with a few sentences sent by Mr. Mate Boban, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which he sent to the then president of the Republic of Croatia, and that's Dr. Franjo Tudjman. His name isn't mentioned, but we know who the president was at the time. On the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see the second page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is an official decision published in the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna which shows that we're talking about a state-like entity, given the fact it has its Official Gazette. So it's a decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It has nine articles. It says that the community is established as a political, cultural, economic, and territorial whole. Then what it's composed of, where the seat is, and it allows for the possibility of accession by other municipalities. And I needn't mention all articles. And the third page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's see the third page in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: There is a list on which we see the signatures of the representatives of individual towns or municipalities that joined the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. These are probably the signatures of these representatives. And the significance of this document is also stated in the footnote, to back up my position that the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ party, as early as 1991, formally established the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a rather broad, regional type of organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina which covers an extensive territory, which we see from the list of the municipalities that joined it. In this chapter, there are more such documents that speak about the foundation and functioning of Herceg-Bosna in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to page 2, and I would like to hear a comment. I'm especially interested in a comment about Article 5 and the reference to the independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna will respect the democratically elected authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for as long as Bosnia and Herzegovina exists as an independent state with regard to the former or any future Yugoslavia. It is said, in other words, that they will respect the existing political and legal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina as long as it's -- as it's part or linked with Yugoslavia. This -- the question what will happen if Bosnia and Herzegovina completely separates itself from Yugoslavia is left open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, when was Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In early 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make a short comment about Article 7 of this document, which says how the supreme body of the community is composed.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It says: "The supreme body of the community shall be the Presidency which shall comprise representatives of the Croatian people in the municipality authorities ..." We see that only "the Croatian people" is mentioned. I believe that the second sentence of this Article is not so important, but it says: "Or the presidents of the municipal boards of the HDZ ..." So this is a fully -- this relies fully on the will of the Croatian Democratic Union, which was one of the victorious parties in the 1990 election.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at tab 28. Your footnote is 93, and the document is 1D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we move on, may I inquire if Mr. Zecevic is going to offer this document? Or is he planning to try and offer all of them at the end of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's 1D141.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This one is 1D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since this document is also part of your report as a footnote, please make a short comment and explain why you considered this document -- you considered it important to mention it in your footnote.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The previous document was dated 18 November as the official date of the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This document shows, and I explained that in paragraph 70 of my expert report, that there already were some forms of regional organisation that were supported by the HDZ. We see from this document that there were at least the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community, which means that this form of regional organisation was typical for the HDZ throughout 1991. This doesn't state when they were created, but their meeting took place on 12 November, six days before the official establishment of Herceg-Bosna, shows that during 1991 there already was some form of regional organisation, some sort of regions. It even says here, this is ultimately 1991, that these regional communities came into being at that time or earlier. That's one thing, one reason why I used this document. And the other is that document states what the final goal of the Croatian people should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's on page 2, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 70, or, yeah, well, in this document it's on page 2; right. And for them, that's the independent Republic of Croatia or the aspiration of the HDZ to establish the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna through the establishment of these regional communities in order to eventually become the Republic of Croatia, territorially speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The following document is tab 34. Your footnote is 149, item 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before we move on, Your Honours, I note in my English translation of paragraph 70 of the report which makes reference to footnote 93, which was the one we're just talking about, it says: "Illegible text M. Bajagic's remark." I wonder if Mr. Zecevic can help us out with what's in the original. Because it appears it hasn't been translated, at least in my English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me -- let me see if I can -- this is -- that should be page 1, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 93. It's paragraph 34 of the English translation. The very last remark under paragraph 70. I'm sorry, it's paragraph 70 on page 34 where there's a reference to footnote 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please explain the following. At the end of paragraph 70 of your report, we see "Illegible text M. Bajagic's remarks" in brackets. Can you please explain what this refers to, which part of the document itself?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It refers to the very last lines on page 1 of the document. That's why I made this remark, because I didn't want to speculate. When something is illegible, then you should state so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the first page. [In English] Mr. Hannis, I must give credit to the CLSS. They have obviously been able to decipher this, but and I also have the problem as Mr. Bajagic has, reading what is written in the last -- last sentence on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following document is tab 34. The document is P1880. Your footnote 149.4. As we see in your footnote, this document, too, is about one of the regional communities that were created in the territory. And please explain why you considered this document important and why you cite it in a footnote in your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, as I pointed out, all the parties, all the key political subjects, made certain moves, and this is the proof that the Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in certain areas, during the year 1991, also, similarly or in the same manner, began to organise itself at the regional level. And this is the decision to promulgate the Autonomous Region of Krajina as a part of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia and the federative unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina as its integral part. And I just think that this document shows fully, which is necessary, that the moves of all sides in the political life at the time have to be taken into account. And here we are discussing the Serbian side. I do not see much difference at first between the Croatian Community in -- of Herceg-Bosna and the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina, and we can see that the tendency existed on all sides. If you would like me to focus on any specific article --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see the time. I would now move to a different subject, so perhaps we might take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. The -- you couldn't make effective use of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, of course I can. I wasn't aware it was ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's 11.57, and we break at 12.05 usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, we could see from the examples which you mentioned about this formation of regional communities you told us that it had a certain impact on the work of the organs of the state in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. How did this regionalisation in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina impact on the abilities and possibilities of central government in Sarajevo to operate? Could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The central authorities in Sarajevo, judging by the division of influence which was a result of the municipality party elections, was made up of all the three sides. But each of the three sides had its own projection of the manner in which it should act in such a context. For these two sides we have shown through documents that they carried out certain activities in order to establish specific regions. I also need to emphasise that this form of organisation had been envisaged in a different legal framework at the time of the former SFRY. And I have to emphasise that Bosnia-Herzegovina, throughout 1991, up until the spring of 1992, was one of the constituent members of the Federation. The Federation was still functional in 1991, and we should bear this in mind. As for the central authorities in Sarajevo, or, rather, the third side in the latent conflicts that were going on at the time, they were not making the moves of this kind; but by trying to become predominant in all the central authorities and institutions, they were trying to achieve their own goals. And through the development of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a civil republic, they were trying to achieve dominance over the other two sides. And this is something is that is present primarily in the first part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You say the third side. Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I have in mind the Party of Democratic Action and the political establishment which represented the Muslim people in the central organs of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for the regional communities, did they also establish their own organs?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The regionals community, and I mean the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, already envisaged the establishment of these organs in their founding documents. And they did establish these organs, the organs which were practically the authorities, and some institutions which looked like state institutions. I think that in certain paragraphs of my expert report, where I discuss the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I mentioned a number of documents in footnotes which talk about appointing certain leaders to specific departments, Department of Justice, Department of the Interior, and Department of Economy, and so on and so forth. The situation was the same on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just be completely clear. We have shown the two examples here, the Herceg-Bosna and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Were there any other autonomous regions or regional communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, there were. In the report there were no examples of the Herzegovina community or the Travnik regional community or some other Serbian autonomous regions, but there were others, evidently. So this was not just, generally speaking, the Herceg-Bosna and the Autonomous Region of Krajina; there were a number of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
