utterances.text: I see the time now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, let us move on to the second part of your report, the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992. That is on page 34. Can you briefly summarise for us what were the characteristics of this period, let me put it that way, this period in the work of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? So after the ethnic parties won the election and the coalition had been formed.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the facts already presented concerning the social atmosphere in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the wake of multi-party elections, the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina found itself in a really complex situation; complex in every sense. We know that, on the basis of the coalition agreement between the three victorious parties, the division of personnel was the same in all state institutions, that is to say that the ethnic-based parties agreed that positions in state organs, including the MUP, should be equally distributed on the basis of the party agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it will be easier, in order to illustrate what we are discussing, if we can have a look at P875. I haven't announced it, but I hope that it will not be a problem. It is a chart provided by the Prosecution which reflects and illustrates the structure of the Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Hannis. [In English] [Microphone not activated] perhaps -- perhaps usher can give this to witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bajagic, please have a look. This is a chart prepared by the Prosecution, and it is supposed to reflect, more or less, the situation between January 1991 and March 1992, as the title says. "The Situation in the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So I would ask you to have a look at it and to confirm whether this is your opinion as well.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see in this chart that the minister of the interior is Mr. Alija Delimustafic, his deputy is Mr. Vitomir Zepinic, and that one of the advisors is Mr. Mico Stanisic. Below that, I see that we have various lines of work, and I can see the names of the officials who were discharging the duties as leaders of these organisational units in the seat of the ministry. And still below that, where we can see the blue signs resembling houses, we can see the organisational structure of the Security Services Centres which existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please -- I apologise for this digression. I wanted us to present this. And, now, please, if you can continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As we can see on this chart, and as I mentioned in my expert report, on the basis of the party agreement, the positions within the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were divided according to the percentage of the influence that the parties had in power. Probably, though I did not deal with that in detail, this was reflected in the territorial principle of organisation from the top down, depending on the areas where a specific party won most votes in the elections in certain areas; there they would get most seats in the organs of power. What is always a problem for any Ministry of the Interior is that it should operate on the principles of political neutrality and professionalism; whereas, the political parties were trying to exert some sort of influence on the personnel policy within the ministry. This is one of my main observations; that in certain situations it is surprising that the parties made such efforts to try and have a dominate influence on the personnel policy within the MUP and it had to be achieved in spite of the grudges of other sides and putting aside the duties which had to be discharged and which are defined by the Law on the Ministry of the Interior. This is one of my observations from this chapter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If -- Mr. Usher, can you please give me back the chart, because it is probably difficult for the expert to deal with all these papers in front of him. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on, Mr. Bajagic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The other observation in connection with this is that the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had to take into account what was happening at the international level and relating to the future destiny of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its state and territorial organisation. I mean the negotiation process which was ongoing under the auspices of the international community. And this was one of the elements that determined the future operation, functioning, and decentralisation of the Minister of the Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is specified in the contents and also in the opinion I provided in certain paragraphs of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, can you clarify for us the notion of what tripartite means, what it means in general, and whether it was applied to the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, tripartite should, in this case, mean that the party agreement is to be strictly observed and that all three political forces should have equal influence on the operation of the Ministry of the Interior. That means everyone is equal. And on the basis of the method of work which was established by consensus, it implies the awareness of all three sides of the main directions of activities of the other two sides. So it means transparency in terms of the influence anyone would have on the work of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your research, did -- this tripartite principle in the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it observed and honoured?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As I pointed out in a number of paragraphs and supported it by sources which are provided in the footnotes, it is clear that the Party of Democratic Action violated the party agreement, not only in terms of appointing personnel or observing the agreement on appointments of high officials at the ministry seat, but they were also carrying out other activities which suggest unlawful meddling with the personnel policy of the Ministry of the Interior of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 106 on page 39 of your expert report, could you please comment on paragraph 106 and the one following it. That's 107.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 106, in order to explain what I stated previously, I talk about instructions on mobilising the police reserve force which was issued on the 26th of September, 1991. The instruction was signed by the then deputy minister of the interior, Mr. Vitomir Zepinic. The instruction was a result of an order of the Presidency. It was a result of the order issued by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Further on in this paragraph, I discuss the dissatisfaction of the Serbian personnel in the MUP concerning the situation, but I have to refer to paragraph 107 where I specify that one of the officials of the MUP in his dispatch said that the mobilisation of the reserve forces of the police was unconstitutional because this order or instruction could only have been issued on the level of the then SFRY, as Bosnia-Herzegovina was still a federal unit of the SFRY at the time. In the dispatch, Mr. Mandic referred to the decision of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1988 pertaining to this issue. Therefore, the instruction on the mobilisation of the police reserve forces which was issued on 26th of September, 1991, considering the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was at the time still a federal unit of the SFRY, was unconstitutional and unlawful.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for the sake of reference, the document that the expert is talking about is Exhibit 1D130 in this case. Mr. Bajagic, this mobilisation of the police reserve forces, as we can see here one of the members of the collegium addressed all the relevant state organs while protesting about this. As you said, this was unconstitutional and unlawful. When you say that it was contrary to the constitution and unlawful, what do you have in mind? Do you have in mind the number or the decision itself or both?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I have both in mind. Simply, the organs of the SFRY and the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina were the organs who could have made such a decision. It had to be taken at the level of the federal state rather than individually by a constituent unit. The fact that really should be taken into account when we analyse any of the processes that took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991 was that it was still formerly at the time a constituent unit of SFRY. Therefore in this territory the laws of SFRY were supposed to be observed in this territory. They were still in force there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will show you a document and ask you for your comment. It's connected with this. It's tab 18, 65 ter 720D1. It's a Defence document. And I need page 18 in the Serbian text. The page number from the book is 157. The next page, please. I apologise. Mr. Bajagic, I will read this to you. I'm just interested in your -- in your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can I confirm we're on the correct page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have that up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. [Interpretation] It seems that this has not been translated. I apologise. We'll return to it later. It seems not to have been translated, and if that is so, then this would make no sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, tell me, calling up the reserve police in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did that cause certain reactions? If so, what were these reactions; and, if you know, why?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents that were accessible to me when working on this expert report and on the basis of this very document that you withdrew just now, the conclusion may be that, in a certain way, calling up the reserve police, the "milicija," in September 1991 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in this way, as it had been done, led to protests from the other sides, especially the Serb personnel in the Ministry of the Interior at the time, because everything pointed to a similar process that had taken place in the Republic of Croatia. The reserve police force was supposed to be the nucleus of some new armed forces, and this is something that stems from various documents. And that is supposed to be the nucleus of the SDA and the future authorities in Sarajevo. And that is why we see these documents of those protests with regard to this fact; namely, calling up the reserve force, and, further on, the mobilisation of the reserve forces, and further activities once the mobilisation had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move to paragraph 3 on page 44, the functioning of the Ministry of Interior in the Serb Republic in 1992, April. Mr. Bajagic, in your paper, in paragraph 127, you listed certain documents. I would like to ask you for your comments in respect of paragraph 127 from your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: In order to speak about the legal framework in terms of the development and functioning of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later Republika Srpska, in the period from April until December 1992, it was important, and that is what I did when writing up this expert report, to carry out a detailed analysis of an entire set of laws that are, at the same time, primary sources when categorising all of the material that this research is based on. I've already mentioned that this is the Constitution, the Law on the Government, the Law on State Administration, the Law on the Interior, the Law on Defence, the Law on the Army. So these are laws that were published in 1992. And, of course, some other laws are mentioned here as well, that follow the development of the ministry on the basis which we can follow the development of this legal framework of the ministry all the way throughout the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it is certain that these four laws - government, state administration, ministries, and especially the Ministry of the Interior - that is what is the most important. In my very own modest view, without analysing these laws, it would be impossible to speak about the genesis, organisation, purview, competencies, powers, and all other matters relevant to the functioning of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By way of a brief illustration, tab 35, your footnote 152. That is P181. It is the Constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The reason why you included the Constitution as the very first document is self-evident, I believe, but could you please explain, nevertheless, why it ranks first on your list of documents.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Of course. When discussing such an important organ of the executive as the ministry is and discussing important system-based laws, we have to look at the top-most legal document, that is, the Constitution, that refers to the rights and responsibilities of the executive, as well as all other branches of government. That is why the Constitution is referred to in my paragraph 131. I directly speak about -- Article 90 of the Constitution, that refers to the rights and responsibilities of the government and makes it in charge of constituting the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to look at a few decisions and to ask you for your comment. Tab number 9. That is 65 ter 468D1. It has to do with paragraphs 91 and 93 of your report. Can you give us your comment with regard to this document that we see in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: As we can see from the document itself, this is a decision on the establishment of the Council for National Security by the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the date is the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Signed by?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly of the Serb People, Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik, who has a master's degree as well. May I proceed? I see that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. We are going to -- just take it easy, will you? Let us not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the establishment of the Council for National Security as an advisory organ of the Assembly that has a purview of its own. The Council is responsible to the Assembly, and there's a reference to the membership of the Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just finish my sentence. So this is the Council for National Security as an advisory body of the Assembly, and the Assembly is a legislative organ, not an executive organ, although, if we take into account world trends, national security councils are usually established by the executive, and they have a purview that is much wider than the one referred to here. It is only the advisory function that is referred to here; whereas, national security councils in the world have other roles, like directing, guiding, and advising in the field of national security. Whereas, here there is only a reference to ... it is the head of the executive that heads the national security councils that exist worldwide today, but here the National Security Council only has an advisory function, and that would be my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D531, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Should this be in the law library?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so, Your Honours. This is the decision by which the Council for National Security has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for the next document that I would like to ask you to comment upon, Mr. Bajagic, we're looking at tab 10. 469D1 is the 65 ter number. Can you give us your brief comment on this document that consists of two parts.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is a decision on declaring a state of imminent threat of war and also this is an order to mobilise the TO in the whole territory of the SBH [as interpreted]. This decision was taken by the Presidency of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina confirmed this decision on the 15th of April, 1992, and it is signed by president of the Assembly of the Serbian People of BH, Momcilo Krajisnik, MA. So the Presidency signed the decision on declaring a state of imminent threat of war and the assembly confirmed this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us be perfectly clear: The date of the decision of the assembly is ... could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It says here, 03-11/92, the 15th of April, 1992. And the session of the Assembly of the Serb People was held on the 12th of May, 1992, and that is when they confirmed this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection. But before we give that a number, Your Honour, going back to the last exhibit, in the light of the question that Judge Harhoff asked, I checked, and it appears that the document we just gave the number Exhibit 1D531 is already in the law library as L-327.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. Let me check this. Just a second. The only way would be if it was published in the Official Gazette. That might be the case. Just bear with me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry. You were right, Mr. Hannis. We checked. It's a part of the law library. Therefore, we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- vacate the number that we just assigned?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, yes, we should vacate the number 1D531, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have no objection to the current proposed exhibit getting that number now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I'm moving that that document, 469D1, be admitted as 1D531.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that would be assigned that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at document tab 46. That is your footnote 326, paragraph 2. And the document is 1D170. Since this document is part of your report, sir, could you please give us your comment. Let us see who signed it. That is on page 2. And let us see the date. And could you please give us your brief comment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is a document, or, rather, decision on establishing the Territorial Defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an armed force. And there is also the accompanying decision on declaring a state of imminent threat of war. It was taken by Minister Bogdan Subotic on the 16th of April, 1992. It was sent to the autonomous region and the Serb autonomous districts or regions in the territory of the Serb Republic of BH. I used the document in paragraph 284, as you can see, right, from the footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to focus on sub-item 2, the decentralisation of the MUP, on page 40 of your report. Paragraphs 109 through 124. The document is under paragraph 24 [as interpreted] and your footnote is number 13. The document itself is 1D78. Could you please comment.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: This is an instruction which is the result of the collegium of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina held on the 1st of April, 1992. At that collegium meeting, as we can see from the text, the decentralisation of the MUP was discussed in accordance with the last round of talks in the framework of the Cutileiro Plan. I must also mention the Sarajevo Agreement, which was reached a few days earlier. The overall context was the plan of the structuring of the state of BH, and three constituent units were to be created and with their respective public administration bodies, including the -- a MUP. So this is a -- this is an instruction from the joint collegium of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you dealt with this, tell me if that plan, known as the Cutileiro Plan, actually, the plan of the EU, and including the Sarajevo Agreement, did it include the establishment of ministries of the interior in their respective entities and a joint MUP or was there a different approach?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: One of the articles of the Sarajevo Agreement envisaged that each constituent unit was entitled to set up its own Ministry of the Interior. And probably at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, some line ministries were joint, among them the Ministry of the Interior. So there was one ministry at the top, and below it, the units had their respective ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the second paragraph of this document on the screen, some names are listed, namely, those present at this MUP collegium, the collegium of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH held on the 1st of April, 1992. I can see that Minister Alija Delimustafic is not listed here. Could you comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't comment, but I see that the deputy minister was present and all highest-ranking officials who are the proper members of the collegium of the MUP, which means those that were appointed by the three parties. There's the under-secretary for the SDB, the assistant minister for the police, and other officials. So a possible comment of mine would be that, having a collegium session even without the presence of the minister himself, who probably had some other urgent commitments elsewhere, does not diminish the significance of this document because of all -- because all other officials were present, representatives of all three parties that made up the highest ranking -- or the highest echelon of officials in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Bajagic, this document envisaged the composition and remit of the expert collegium of the MUP, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: That -- well, that follows from the Law on the Interior of the SRBH and the rule-book on the internal organisation of the ministry. I believe that rule-book was adopted in 1994, that single MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm about to show you this bylaw, the rule-book, tab 138. Your footnote is 168. And the exhibit number is P850. No, this isn't it. P850. 65 ter 02668. 65 ter list of the OTP. Sir, is this the rule-book you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since which year was this rule-book in use; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: We see that the date here is from the 29th of January, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this rule-book in use in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The internal organisation of the MUP of the Serb Republic of BH was made pursuant to this rule-book, until a new rule-book was adopted. That is, until the adoption of the rule-book on the internal organisation of the MUP of the Serb Republic of BH throughout 1992, this one was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us sum up then. This is the rule-book on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior, which at the time was called Republican Secretariat of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you say that it was in force since 29 January 1990?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this rule-book used in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the 29th of January, 1990, and April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a rule-book that regulated the internal organisation of the Secretariat of the Interior, which later became the MUP, of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us already that this same rule-book was also in use in the MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina until the adoption of the rule-book of the SRBH. Tell us, when was the latter, the rule-book of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, adopted?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: It was adopted in the first quarter of 1993. I think it was late April or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction late March or early April.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Which means that this rule-book was in force. And throughout 1992, that is, during the establishment of the organisational structure of the MUP of the Serb Republic of BH, was governed by its provisions. The Constitution of the Serb Republic stipulates that all laws and regulations that are not in direct contradiction of the Constitution will remain in force, irrespective if we're -- whether we're speaking about laws or bylaws or subordinate legislation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please make another comment for us. Page 287, ERN 0113-7325. In the header of your copy, you will find page number 284. Paragraph 126, criminal logs.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there is a translation of this OTP document. I'm not sure there is one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you explain what we see in items 126, 127, 128, 129, and 130. They deal with various types of logs. Could you list them for us and explain what kind of logs they are.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: They are operative log-books of the Ministry of the Interior; that is, criminal, operative, and investigative, as well as misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Please list for us every log-book and tell us to which line of work it is linked.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The first one is the criminal log-book. It is a log-book based on the -- on the decisions of domestic and foreign courts. That is, persons are entered here who are convicted by courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a widely known as the KE log-book.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the ministry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, please make a pause between question and answer. I'm trying to clarify things. In this way, we can create an even greater problem in the transcript. So this is -- what -- what is this called in the police jargon?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: You have just said it, the KE.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The following log-books are operative crime investigation log-books, and I don't think there's a need for me to list them all. The first log-book, the criminal log-book, shows the administrative function of the ministry and its wide remit. The third log-book is the operative MOS evidence. Just like the operative and the criminal investigation log-book, it has to do with the crime investigation service of the ministry and other connected units. The following log-book is the misdemeanours log-book. It's on the following page. Where the Ministry of the Interior keeps this log-book based on the decisions of misdemeanour courts, with the perpetrators of those misdemeanours. And, finally, there's the criminal register. This is a register kept by the Ministry of Interior as a summary of all lines of work. That is, the drafting of criminal complaints against known and unknown perpetrators of crimes. And then there are various ways of keeping registers, by persons, by types of criminal offences, and so on. And we needn't go into that. So this is the last type of register mentioned in this rule-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what's the abbreviated name of that register in the police jargon?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, criminal register. I don't know. I can't remember any special abbreviated name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I say KU register.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, KU, K-U. These are the initial letters. And the one under item 127 was usually called OE in police jargon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us see page 0113-7510. In the header, you can see page reference 469. And it refers to the professional collegium of the republican secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm being informed that this can be found on the 243rd page of the English text. In Serbian, the page number could be 472. As I said, the ERN is E0113-7510. This is it. I'm told that in English the page number is 243.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please give us a short review about this professional collegium of the republican secretary. First of all, is it the same as the professional collegium of the MUP? And who are the members? And which matters does this body deal with?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: According to these rules, and according to other rules as well, the professional collegium of the republican secretary is the same as the professional collegium of the minister of the interior. It's just a question of changing the name of the ministry. Professional collegiums are always composed of the top professionals of the ministry. The minister is the word I'm going to use now. So it's the minister, the assistant ministers, the heads of the key departments, lines of work, heads of sectors, because at that time, as well, there were two basic sectors within the ministry, one for public security, and the other one for state security. Sometimes these meetings can be attended by other top personnel from the ministry, depending on the agenda. At any rate, this is the highest professional body, and these are the top officials anyway, if we look at the composition of the body. If we look at the questions that they deal with, it has to do with the overall policy of the Ministry of the Interior. Questions related to the implementation of the basic guide-lines provided by the top state authorities, questions related to the strategy and tasks from the line of work of the ministry. Of course, organisational matters as well. Then questions involving the active participation of the ministry in providing draft laws, bills, as well as internal documents that are only drafted by the ministry, and many other questions. We can see that here. I don't have to go into all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the document is self-explanatory, isn't it? Tell me, in your opinion, the previous document that we saw, dated the 1st of April, 1992, the minutes from the collegium, in your opinion does that belong to questions that are discussed by the collegium of the minister of the interior on the basis of these rules?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the items on the agenda of the collegium meeting of the 1st of April, 1992, are questions that the professional collegium of the Ministry of the Interior should deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to show you another document. However, before that, let me ask you: In your opinion, such a record, or, rather, such communication from the collegium meeting of the 1st of April which was sent to all, as far as we can see, including all centres, all public security stations, and the entire top personnel of both ministries, in your view could this document have been sent from the Ministry of the Interior without the agreement or knowledge of the top personnel of that ministry?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: Well, that's impossible. It's impossible for a document of such significance -- and it was a vital issue that was discussed at that collegium meeting, namely, the future functioning of the entire field of the interior in Bosnia-Herzegovina as such. So we're not only talking about the ministry itself. That kind of document could not have left the ministry headquarters without the knowledge of the top officials. The fact that the deputy minister is there and all the other highest officials were there, all of the people comprising this professional collegium on the basis of the rules, indicates that when this document was sent, it meant that the facts referred to in this document were actually accepted by all persons present at that meeting. We do see that the minister was not present at the meeting, but it is impossible to assume that the minister did not know about the content of this meeting because it was attended by his deputy and other top personnel of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you tab 42, your footnote 206. This is document 1D138. Since you cited this document in your report - that's in paragraph 169 - could you please give us a brief comment? We have four minutes left today.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The document I see here is a dispatch sent from the ministry headquarters, and it was sent by Alija Delimustafic, minister of the interior. And in this document, everything that is contained in the document of the 1st of April is categorically refuted. He is completely denying the fact that this collegium was held at all and that certain conclusions had been reached. And, specifically, this document says -- or, rather, he assesses that there was pressure and blackmail, and he is also saying that there were declarations of loyalty that were made. It is a denial issued nine days later by the minister of the interior, and it has to do with the document that had been sent nine days before that. That's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now we go back to the question of the methodology of conclusions. We have discussed that already. So, in this case, we have two documents that are opposites. On the one hand, we have the record of the collegium meeting; and, on the other, this document, dated the 10th of April, which de facto denies everything that is stated in the previous document dated the 1st of April. On which basis do you draw your conclusions, the ones that you refer to here in paragraphs 169, 170, and - how should I put this? - what is the methodology that you used for drawing these conclusions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC
utterances.text: The instruction on information - that is what the dispatch is called - of the 1st of April, 1992, is the result of that collegium meeting, and it is based on the Sarajevo Agreement, on a Bosnia-Herzegovina consisting of three constituent units and the right of these constituent units to have their own Ministries of the Interior. So that document is based on the Cutileiro Plan, the Sarajevo Agreement, and accepting the fact that all persons present at that collegium meeting accept as a fact that this agreement had been reached in Sarajevo. That is what we have on the one hand. It is my assessment that it has a particular, specific weight. On the other hand, this is a dispatch of the minister of the interior, so it is the minister. He knew of the fact that the Sarajevo Agreement had been reached and that a collegium meeting had been held, but in this dispatch he is denying certain things that had started happening on the ground on the basis of the instructions provided in this dispatch sent on 1st of April, 1992. If we are talking about this on scales, as it were, I don't think that this dispatch has the same weight that the previous document has, and that is why I draw the conclusions that are referred to in the relevant paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it would be convenient if we would adjourn for the day. Thank you, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Bajagic, we are about to take the first adjournment for the day in the course of your testimony, which you would have gathered, from what Judge Delvoie said at the beginning, is going to go over several days. You, having testified before this Tribunal previously, I'm reminding you of the fact that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side until at the conclusion of your testimony you are released by the Court. And, furthermore, in such conversations that you may with other persons, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we rise for the day, and we will resume in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
